newsitem.title: UK: Study finds we owe the Earth $33 trillion a year.
newsitem.headline: Study finds we owe the Earth $33 trillion a year.

text.p: The Earth gives us at least $33 trillion worth of "free" materials including air, water and food every year, a team of ecologists and economists said on Wednesday.

The team, sponsored by the National Centre for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis in Santa Barbara, California and headed by Robert Costanza at the University of Maryland, reckoned the value of the air, sea, rivers and even the rocks.

"For the entire biosphere, the value (most of which is outside the market) is estimated to be in the range of $16 to $54 trillion per year, with an average of $33 trillion per year," they wrote, adding: "This must be considered a minimum estimate."
This compared to a global gross national product (GNP) -- the value of all goods and services produced by people -- of $18 trillion.

"The economies of the Earth would grind to a halt without the services of ecological life-support systems, so in one sense their total value to the economy is infinite," they wrote in an article for the science journal Naure.
Nonetheless, they said, it would be useful to examine this value.
So they gathered several recent studies, analysed and put the information into a "form useful for ecologists, economists, policy makers and the general public."
They broke their analysis down by biological sectors. So, for example, the forests provide $141 worth of atmospheric gas regulation per hectare per year.

They also provide climate and disturbance regulation, water regulation and supply, soil formation and erosion control, nutrient cycling, waste treatment, biological control, food production, raw materials, genetic resources, recreation and cultural enjoyment to the tune of $969 per hectare per year.
"If ecosystem services were actually paid for, in terms of their value contribution to the global economy, the global price system would be very different from what it is today," they wrote.
"As natural capital and ecosystem services become more stressed and more 'scarce' in the future, we can only expect their value to increase," they added.

"Nevertheless, even the crude initial estimate we have been able to assemble is a useful starting point...It also highlights the relative importance of ecosystem services and the potential impact on our welfare of continuing to squander them."
Stuart Pimm of the University of Tennessee saw immediate practical applications.

"For example, a proposed project in southwestern Brazil and adjacent countries would straighten and deepen the rivers and so drain many of the surrounding wetlands -- the Pantanal," he wrote in a commentary.
"The value of the increased quantities of soybeans that will be marketed is a simple calculation, but a grossly incomplete evaluation of the project's consequences."
